title: PSALM 23 WAS NEVER JUST FOR FUNERALS: THE TERRIFYINGLY BEAUTIFUL TRUTH HIDDEN IN THE SHEPHERD PSALM
paragraphs: PSALM 23 WAS NEVER JUST FOR FUNERALS: THE TERRIFYINGLY BEAUTIFUL TRUTH HIDDEN IN THE SHEPHERD PSALM
You may have heard it beside a coffin. David wrote it for people who were still breathing—and still walking through valleys.
There is something almost tragic about the way many people first encounter Psalm 23.
They hear it when somebody dies.

A pastor stands beside a grieving family. Flowers surround a coffin. Someone is trying not to cry. Someone else is staring at the floor because looking at the photograph of the person they lost hurts too much.
Then come the familiar words:
“The LORD is my shepherd…”
And because generations of us have heard Psalm 23 in moments like these, we can unconsciously begin treating it as though David wrote a funeral poem.
He didn’t.
Psalm 23 certainly speaks powerfully into death, grief, and mortality.
But it was written for the living.
For frightened people.
For exhausted people.
For people being pursued.
For people surrounded by enemies.
For people who have discovered that following God does not mean avoiding every dark valley.

And perhaps that is why Psalm 23 becomes much more unsettling—and much more beautiful—when you stop reading it as something meant merely to comfort you when someone dies and begin reading it as something meant to teach you how to live while everything around you feels like it is falling apart.
The Hebrew begins:
מִזְמוֹר לְדָוִד יְהוָה רֹעִי לֹא אֶחְסָר
Mizmor leDavid. YHWH ro‘i, lo echsar.
“A psalm of David. The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not lack.”
Slow down.
David does not merely say God is a shepherd.
He makes it personal.
יְהוָה רֹעִי
YHWH ro‘i.
“The LORD is my shepherd.”
That little word changes everything.
Because sheep do not merely admire shepherds.
They depend upon them.
A sheep separated from its shepherd is not experiencing independence. It is experiencing danger.
And suddenly Psalm 23 asks a question considerably more uncomfortable than, “Do you believe in God?”
It asks:
Who is actually shepherding your life?
Because something is.
Your appetite can shepherd you.
Money can shepherd you.
Approval can shepherd you.
Sexual desire can shepherd you.
Resentment can shepherd you.
Fear can shepherd you.
Your political tribe can shepherd you.
Your career can shepherd you.
Your trauma can shepherd you.
Your phone can shepherd you.
Even your desperate need to make everybody think you are okay can shepherd you.
We live in a culture obsessed with independence, yet almost everyone is following something.
David's freedom begins with surrender.
“The LORD is my shepherd.”
Not my feelings.
Not my cravings.
Not the crowd.
Not my past.
Not even myself.
The LORD.
And then comes the declaration:
לֹא אֶחְסָר
Lo echsar.
“I shall not lack.”
That does not mean the believer will receive everything he wants.
David's own life destroys that interpretation.
He experienced danger, betrayal, family catastrophe, warfare, grief, sin, consequences, enemies, and seasons of profound anguish.
Psalm 23 is not prosperity theology hiding inside beautiful poetry.
David is saying something deeper.
If the Shepherd is truly enough, then even when life removes things from me, it cannot remove the One upon whom my soul ultimately depends.
That is why the next line is so beautiful:
בִּנְאוֹת דֶּשֶׁא יַרְבִּיצֵנִי
“He makes me lie down in green pastures.”
Notice something almost uncomfortable.
“He makes me lie down.”
Some of us know exactly what it is like to refuse rest.
We keep moving because silence makes us think.
We keep working because stopping makes us feel.
We keep scrolling because being alone with our thoughts feels unbearable.
We stay busy because somewhere beneath the noise there is grief we haven't processed, sin we haven't confessed, forgiveness we haven't extended, or emptiness we haven't wanted to admit.
And sometimes the Shepherd loves His sheep enough to interrupt them.
The interruption may not feel loving while it is happening.
A closed door.
A season of waiting.
A plan that collapses.
A relationship that exposes what is inside you.
A moment when your strength finally reaches its limit.
Not every hardship should be simplistically described as God “making you lie down.” Scripture does not authorize us to call every tragedy a direct divine intervention.
But Scripture does teach us that God can meet His people in weakness and use suffering without being defeated by it.
And some people reading this know the strange mercy of finally reaching the place where they could no longer pretend they were strong.
You thought you were falling apart.
But perhaps, in that place, you finally stopped running long enough to hear the Shepherd.
Then David writes:
עַל־מֵי מְנֻחוֹת יְנַהֲלֵנִי
Al mei menuchot yenahaleni.
“He leads me beside waters of rest.”
Not waters of panic.
Not waters of endless striving.
Rest.
But then Psalm 23 says something commonly translated:
“He restores my soul.”
The Hebrew is:
נַפְשִׁי יְשׁוֹבֵב
Nafshi yeshovev.
The word nefesh can speak of one's life, self, or living being—not merely “soul” in the later popular sense of an invisible component trapped inside a body.
David is describing restoration at the level of the person.
God brings back what has become depleted.
He revives.
He restores.
He turns the wandering life back toward Himself.
Maybe you need that more than you have admitted.
Because there is a kind of exhaustion sleep cannot cure.
You can sleep eight hours and wake up tired.
You can take a vacation and remain empty.
You can laugh with friends and drive home feeling strangely hollow.
You can sit inside a church while your heart feels miles away from God.
You can even post Bible verses while secretly losing the battle nobody online knows you are fighting.
And that is where Psalm 23 stops being decoration and becomes confrontation.
The Shepherd does not merely want to improve your circumstances.
He wants you.
“He leads me in paths of righteousness for His name's sake.”
The Shepherd comforts—but He also leads.
And His leading has moral direction.
Righteousness.
That means Psalm 23 cannot honestly be reduced to:
“God loves me, therefore I can continue living however I want.”
No.
Grace does not merely soothe wandering sheep.
Grace brings wandering sheep home.
Jesus did not go to the cross so we could decorate our rebellion with Christian vocabulary.
He came to save sinners.
Forgive sinners.
Cleanse sinners.
Transform sinners.
And call sinners to follow Him.
Then the landscape changes.
The pasture disappears.
The quiet water disappears.
Suddenly David is walking somewhere terrifying.
גַּם כִּי־אֵלֵךְ בְּגֵיא צַלְמָוֶת
Gam ki elekh begei tsalmavet…
“Even though I walk through a valley of deepest darkness…”
The famous traditional translation says:
“the valley of the shadow of death.”
And that translation has comforted countless grieving people.
But the Hebrew expression צַלְמָוֶת (tsalmavet) can carry the broader sense of deep or deathlike darkness.
That matters.
Because this valley is not reserved for the cemetery.
You can walk through tsalmavet while still alive.
The diagnosis.
The divorce papers.
The betrayal.
The depression nobody sees.
The night your child calls crying.
The financial collapse.
The temptation you thought you had conquered.
The funeral you were not ready to attend.
The prayer that seems unanswered.
The season when heaven appears silent.
The moment you look at your own life and whisper:
“How did I get here?”
Psalm 23 never promises you will not enter that valley.
Read that again.
God never promised His sheep a valley-free existence.
Christianity does not mean Jesus hands you a map around suffering.
Sometimes He leads you through it.
But there is one word in the verse that changes the entire valley.
עִמָּדִי
Immadi.
“With me.”
“I will fear no evil, for You are with me.”
David's confidence is not that the valley isn't dangerous.
His confidence is that he isn't abandoned.
And there is something extraordinary happening grammatically and relationally in the psalm.
Before the valley, David speaks about God.
“He makes me…”
“He leads me…”
“He restores…”
Then inside the darkness, David begins speaking to God.
“You are with me.”
“Your rod…”
“Your staff…”
Sometimes suffering turns theology into prayer.
It is easy to talk about God beside green pastures.
The valley teaches you to talk to Him.
And perhaps you know exactly what that feels like.
There are prayers you pray when life is comfortable.
And there are prayers you pray at 2:17 in the morning when nobody else is awake.
“Jesus…”
That is sometimes the whole prayer.
“Jesus, help me.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Jesus, don't let me go.”
“Jesus, I don't know what to do.”
And somehow the Shepherd hears prayers that barely have enough strength to become sentences.
David continues:
“Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me.”
We often imagine comfort as softness.
But shepherding included protection and guidance.
The Shepherd's comfort is not sentimental indulgence.
Sometimes His protection comforts.
Sometimes His correction comforts.
That means one of the most loving things God can do is refuse to let us comfortably destroy ourselves.
Some of us pray:
“Lord, lead me.”
But what we mean is:
“Lord, approve the direction I already chose.”
Those are not the same prayer.
The Shepherd has a staff because sheep wander.
And this is where Psalm 23 points us beyond David toward Jesus Christ.
Centuries later Jesus would say:
“I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.”
Do not miss how shocking that is.
Psalm 23 says:
“The LORD is my shepherd.”
Then in John 10 Jesus identifies Himself as the Good Shepherd and describes His mission in terms of laying down His life for the sheep.
The Shepherd enters the danger.
The Shepherd bears the cost.
The Shepherd gives His life.
And at the cross we discover just how far the Shepherd is willing to go to rescue sinners.
Jesus did not merely stand outside our darkness shouting directions.
He entered human suffering.
He was betrayed.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Rejected.
Crucified.
And He bore sin so that guilty people could be reconciled to God.
The Shepherd became the sacrifice.
And death did not get the final word.
Christ rose.
That is why Christian hope is not:
“Nothing bad will happen to me.”
Christian hope is:
Whatever happens, Jesus Christ has already walked into death and come out victorious.
Then Psalm 23 changes scenes again.
“You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies.”
Notice what God does not necessarily do first.
He does not immediately remove the enemies.
He prepares a table while they are still there.
Imagine it.
Danger nearby.
Enemies watching.
And God says:
Sit.
Eat.
You are under My care.
There is something almost defiant about that peace.
Biblical peace is not always the absence of conflict.
Sometimes it is the presence of God in the middle of conflict.
Your enemies do not get to determine whether God can sustain you.
Your critics do not get to cancel God's faithfulness.
Your past does not get the final vote on your future.
Your worst chapter does not get to write the ending.
And your scandal does not have authority greater than His grace.
That does not mean consequences disappear.
David knew consequences.
Repentance does not magically erase every earthly result of our decisions.
But grace means your sin does not have to become your final identity.
Peter denied Jesus.
Thomas doubted.
Paul had persecuted Christians.
The woman at the well carried a complicated history.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left with which to repair his reputation.
Yet Christ kept rewriting stories.
Not by pretending sin was harmless.
By dealing with sin through grace.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Then David says:
“You anoint my head with oil; my cup overflows.”
Not barely enough.
Overflow.
Not because David's circumstances were always easy.
Because the Shepherd's goodness was greater than the wilderness.
And then comes perhaps one of the most misunderstood beautiful lines in the entire psalm:
“Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life.”
The Hebrew says:
אַךְ טוֹב וָחֶסֶד יִרְדְּפוּנִי
Akh tov va-chesed yirdefuni.
Goodness and chesed.
חֶסֶד — chesed.
A word rich with the idea of steadfast, faithful, covenant love.
But look at the verb:
יִרְדְּפוּנִי
yirdefuni.
It can mean pursue me.
Not merely casually follow several steps behind.
Pursue.
David knew what being pursued felt like.
Enemies had pursued him.
Danger had pursued him.
Consequences had pursued him.
But David reaches the end of Psalm 23 and realizes:
Something else has been chasing me.
God's goodness.
God's steadfast love.
Perhaps you have spent years believing your past is chasing you.
Perhaps shame keeps whispering:
“You will always be what you did.”
Perhaps your memories keep replaying the person you used to be.
Perhaps there is something you have never told anyone because you are terrified that if people knew the entire story, they would never look at you the same way again.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not tell you that your sin was insignificant.
The Gospel tells you that Christ's blood is sufficient.
Repentance means we stop defending our sin and bring it into the light before God.
Grace means the sinner who comes to Christ does not find a Savior reluctant to forgive.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Maybe this article found you while you are walking through your valley.
Maybe everyone thinks you are doing fine.
Maybe you have mastered the smile.
The church smile.
The family smile.
The Facebook smile.
But God knows what happens after the screen goes dark.
He knows what you cried about.
He knows what you are afraid of.
He knows what you did.
He knows what was done to you.
He knows what you keep trying to forget.
He knows the temptation.
He knows the secret.
He knows the exhaustion.
And still the Shepherd calls.
Not:
“Clean yourself up enough and perhaps I will receive you.”
But:
“Come.”
Repent.
Believe.
Follow Me.
You may have spent years running from God only to discover that His mercy has been pursuing you through every mile.
If this exposed something hidden in you, don't hide behind religious language.

And if you have lived long enough to know that your worst chapter was not your final chapter, tell somebody what Jesus has done. Your testimony may become the sentence God uses to make another wounded person realize they are not alone.
Send this to the person who has stopped talking about what hurts.
And stay close to Gospel Warrior if you want daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
We glorify God through faith, worship, obedience, love, generosity, holiness, and lives surrendered to Christ.
But supporting faithful Gospel work can itself become one practical expression of generosity and partnership in ministry.
Not to glorify an algorithm.
Not to glorify Gospel Warrior.
Not to glorify yourself.
Because somewhere tonight somebody is walking through tsalmavet.
Deep darkness.
They are wondering whether God abandoned them.
They are wondering whether their sin disqualified them.
They are wondering whether they can ever come home.
And perhaps what they need is not another motivational quote.
Perhaps they need to hear:
The Shepherd is still calling.
The Shepherd still restores.
The Shepherd still leads.
The Shepherd still corrects.
The Shepherd still protects.
The Shepherd still prepares tables in hostile territory.
The Shepherd still pursues His people with goodness and steadfast love.
And Jesus Christ—the Good Shepherd—still saves sinners.
Psalm 23 was never merely a beautiful passage to read when somebody's journey ends.
It is a declaration for those of us whose journey is still happening.
For the pasture.
For the wilderness.
For the table.
For the enemy.
For the failure.
For the restoration.
For the valley.
Even for the grave.
Because the Christian does not walk into darkness alone.
The Shepherd has already gone ahead.
And maybe that is what you need to remember tonight:
The valley may become part of your story, but because of Jesus, the valley never gets to be your Shepherd.
